title: Rachmaninoff and Richter: bells become a song
work: Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 18 — I. Moderato, opening-side comparison only
question: How do Rachmaninoff and Richter make the piano sing after its opening chords and rushing accompaniment?
intro: The piano’s opening chords toll like bells, then break into running notes beneath a melody for strings and clarinet. Before long the soloist takes a song of its own in E♭ major. Rachmaninoff’s 1929 Philadelphia performance and Richter’s 1959 Warsaw recording meet here over the opening disc side.

recordings.label: Rachmaninoff, Stokowski, Philadelphia Orchestra, 1929
recordings.note: Recorded at Philadelphia’s Academy of Music on 10 April 1929; the published opening comes from the third take.

recordings.label: Richter, Wisłocki, Warsaw Philharmonic, 1959
recordings.note: Richter and Wisłocki made this complete concerto recording with the Warsaw Philharmonic for Deutsche Grammophon.

passages.label: The orchestra sings, the piano runs
passages.note: Violins, violas and clarinet carry the C minor tune. The piano sweeps through broken chords beneath them, above plucked cellos and basses.

passages.label: The piano steps forward
passages.note: The piano steps out from beneath the strings, running between held woodwind chords and short orchestral replies.

passages.label: The piano’s E♭ major song
passages.note: The piano takes the second melody in E♭ major, singing above its own broken chords. Quiet strings and brief wind replies leave room around it.
